title: Monks as keepers
hookLine: as Rome fell, monasteries copied and kept books

cards: How does a book outlast the world that made it? One answer sits at a sloping desk, with a quill, a pot of ink, and a sheet of animal skin scraped smooth.
A monk bends over it, copying one letter at a time from an older book propped beside him. His back aches. His fingers are stained.
The light from the window is fading. Outside the walls, the old Roman world is coming apart. Inside, he finishes a line, checks it against the original, and dips the pen again.

teach.b: A scriptorium is a monastery's writing room, where monks copied books by hand.

Why did monks need books at all? Benedict's Rule, which we met yesterday, sets aside hours every day for reading. And in Lent, it says, each monk is to receive a book from the library and read it straight through.
So a monastery needed a library, and a library needs copies. Next, a man who praised copying as holy work. Cassiodorus founded a monastery called Vivarium.
In his book of instructions for its monks, he praises the copyist above almost any other kind of manual labor.

The copyist, he says, preaches to people with his hand, and spreads the Lord's words to faraway places without leaving his seat. Every word copied, he says, is a wound to the devil. Now, what they kept.
Scripture first: the Gospels, the Psalms, the whole Bible. Then the Fathers: Augustine, Jerome, the ones we've been meeting these past weeks.
And alongside them, some readers point out, the monks also copied grammar books and works of pagan authors, because you needed good Latin to read scripture well.
The world outside could be loud and violent and falling apart, and inside, someone was sitting at a desk, making sure the next generation would have something to read. Not by fighting.
By sitting still and copying, line after line, in a room set apart for it. When you open a Bible today, part of its long road ran through rooms like that one.

how: Catholic monasteries kept libraries and copied books by hand, and Benedictine communities still set aside daily hours for sacred reading, called lectio divina.

games.why: Cassiodorus says the copyist preaches with his hand and sends the Lord's words to places he'll never see.

practice: Find a pen and any scrap of paper, and choose one line worth keeping: a verse, a line from a prayer you know, a sentence someone once said to you that stayed.
Write it slowly, letter by letter, the way the monk at the desk did, then read it once, quietly, and check it against where it came from. If you pray, let the line you copied become your prayer.
